chapter_summary:
Welcome to the heart of Unity development: the Unity Editor. This integrated development environment (IDE) is where you'll spend most of your time building, testing, and refining your games. Mastering its interface is the first crucial step towards becoming a proficient Unity programmer. The editor is designed to be highly flexible, allowing you to arrange its various windows and panels to suit your personal workflow.

At its core, the Unity Editor is composed of several key windows, each serving a distinct purpose. The **Scene view** is your primary workspace, a 3D canvas where you visually construct your game world. Here, you can place objects, arrange them, and design levels. Think of it as your director's chair, giving you a bird's-eye view (or any view you desire) of your entire set. You navigate the Scene view using a combination of mouse and keyboard controls: holding the right mouse button and moving the mouse allows you to look around, while the W, A, S, D keys move you forward, left, backward, and right, respectively. Q and E keys move you up and down. Using the middle mouse button (or Alt + left mouse button) allows you to pan, and the scroll wheel zooms in and out. A common mistake beginners make is struggling with navigation; practice these controls until they become second nature.

Adjacent to the Scene view, or often docked next to it, is the **Game view**. This window represents what the player sees through the camera(s) in your game. It's crucial for testing and previewing your game in real-time. While the Scene view allows you to manipulate objects freely, the Game view shows the actual runtime output, including lighting, post-processing effects, and UI elements. It's important to remember that changes made in the Scene view are immediately reflected in the Game view (if the game is not running), but changes made *during play mode* in the Scene view are temporary and will revert once you exit play mode. This is a common pitfall: spending time tweaking values in play mode only to lose them. Always make sure you're not in play mode when making permanent adjustments.

On the left side of the editor, you'll typically find the **Hierarchy window**. This window lists every GameObject currently present in your active scene. It's an organized tree structure, showing parent-child relationships between objects. For instance, a character model might be a child of an empty GameObject that controls its overall movement, or a weapon might be a child of a character's hand. This hierarchical structure is fundamental for organizing complex scenes and managing transformations (movement, rotation, scale) where child objects inherit transformations from their parents.

Below the Hierarchy, you'll encounter the **Project window**. This is your asset browser, displaying all the files and folders that make up your game project – scripts, 3D models, textures, audio clips, animations, and more. It mirrors the file structure on your hard drive within your project's `Assets` folder. Keeping this window organized with a clear folder structure (e.g., `Scripts`, `Models`, `Materials`, `Audio`) is vital for project maintainability, especially as your game grows in complexity. Dragging assets from your operating system's file explorer directly into the Project window is a quick way to import them.

To the right, the **Inspector window** is arguably one of the most frequently used panels. When you select a GameObject in the Hierarchy or an asset in the Project window, the Inspector displays all its properties and components. For GameObjects, this includes its Transform component (position, rotation, scale) and any custom scripts or built-in components attached to it. For assets, it shows import settings and previews. This is where you'll adjust variables, configure component behaviors, and fine-tune almost everything about your game objects and assets. Understanding how to read and modify properties in the Inspector is key to configuring your game without writing extensive code.

Finally, the **Console window** is your debugging lifeline. It displays messages, warnings, and errors generated by Unity or your scripts. When something goes wrong in your code, or if you use `Debug.Log()` to print information, it will appear here. Learning to interpret console messages is an invaluable skill for troubleshooting. A red error message indicates a critical problem that often prevents your game from running correctly, while yellow warnings suggest potential issues that might lead to problems later. Always keep an eye on your console.

Unity's layout is highly customizable. You can drag and drop any window to reposition it, dock it, or even float it as a separate window. You can save custom layouts (Window > Layouts > Save Layout...) to quickly switch between configurations optimized for level design, scripting, animation, or UI work. This flexibility allows you to create an environment that maximizes your productivity. For example, a common layout for scripting might involve having the Scene view and Game view side-by-side, with the Hierarchy and Project windows on the left, and the Inspector and Console windows on the right, providing quick access to all essential tools.

screens.title: Navigating the Unity Editor Interface
screens.subtitle: Master the core windows, navigation, and workspace habits you'll use every day.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn the essential portions of the Unity Editor so you can move confidently from design to testing. The Editor is where you assemble scenes, inspect objects, manage assets, and read runtime feedback. Knowing which window to use and how the Scene and Game views relate will save you time and prevent common mistakes, like losing changes made during Play Mode. You will see concrete controls for moving the camera, for moving and transforming objects, and for organizing assets in the Project window. We'll also cover practical workflow habits: how to use the Hierarchy to structure objects, how to read the Inspector to tune components, and how the Console helps you debug. By the end you will be able to create a cube, move it with the transform tools, frame a selection, and save a custom layout tailored to your task. As you progress, test small changes outside Play Mode and practice the navigation keybindings until they feel natural. Think of the Editor as your workspace: learning its windows and shortcuts is like learning how to arrange and use your tools efficiently. Ready to explore the core topics that make Unity productive and predictable?

keyIdea.title: Editor as your primary workspace
keyIdea.text: Mastering the Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, Inspector, and Console makes development quicker and reduces costly mistakes like losing Play Mode edits.

Navigating the Unity Editor Interface
Quick orientation to the windows and controls you'll use every day.
What you'll practice

Why it matters
Good navigation and window use prevents wasted time and accidental loss of edits while testing in Play Mode.
Explore Key Topics
Scene & Game Views
Design in Scene, preview in Game to see camera output and post-processing effects.
Inspector & Hierarchy
Use Hierarchy to structure objects and Inspector to tune components and transforms.
Project & Console
Organize assets in Project and watch Console for logs, warnings, and errors while testing.
Concept Snapshot
Scene: interactive 3D workspace for arranging objects and composing levels.
Game: the runtime camera output used for testing the player's view and final rendering.
Play Mode: temporary runtime state; changes made while running are not saved after you stop.
Key Takeaway

Treat the Editor as a workspace: learn windows, practice navigation, and avoid editing permanent values during Play Mode.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll master in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will identify the Editor windows and explain their purpose, navigate the Scene view confidently, manipulate GameObjects with transform tools, and customize your layout for efficient workflows. First, you will learn to name the six core windows and describe why each exists: Scene for building, Game for runtime preview, Hierarchy for scene structure, Project for assets, Inspector for properties, and Console for debugging. Knowing the purpose of each helps you pick the right tool for a task. Next, you will practice camera controls: orbit, pan, zoom, and frame selection, which let you inspect details and position objects precisely. Then you will use the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools and observe how Transform values update in the Inspector — an essential link between visual edits and numeric values. Finally, you will be able to drag, dock, and save a custom Editor layout so your environment matches tasks like level design or scripting. Each objective includes a short practice step to reinforce learning and a small mnemonic to recall the window roles. These skills reduce frustration and improve iteration speed, which is why we prioritize them early in your Unity workflow.

keyIdea.title: Practical goals
keyIdea.text: Identify key windows, master camera and transform controls, and save a custom layout to streamline development.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Steps
screens.subtitle: Concrete practice tasks to build muscle memory and project hygiene

narration.text: This screen gives practical steps you can perform immediately to turn knowledge into habit. First, create a new 3D project and find each core window: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, Inspector, Console. Naming them helps you reach for the correct tool. Second, practice Scene navigation in short bursts: look around with the right mouse button plus mouse movement, move with the W-A-S-D keys, and use Q and E to lift or lower your view. Add the middle mouse button pan and scroll wheel zoom. Try framing the Main Camera with the F key so you understand precisely how to center a selection. Third, create a cube (GameObject > 3D Object > Cube), and use W, E, and R to Move, Rotate, and Scale. Watch the Transform values update in the Inspector and repeat until the controls are smooth. Fourth, customize a layout by docking the Console near the Project window and saving your layout as a named preset. Each practice step reduces friction and prevents the common error of making permanent changes while in Play Mode. These short, repeatable exercises are the fastest route to confidently using the Editor daily.

keyIdea.title: Practice builds reliable habits
keyIdea.text: Short, repeated exercises—create a cube, move/rotate/scale, frame selections, and save a layout—make navigation and editing second nature.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Practice Steps
Starter checklist
  1. Open a new 3D Core project and locate the six core windows visually.
  2. Create a Cube and watch the Transform component change as you edit.
  3. Practice camera controls: orbit, pan, zoom, WASD movement, and frame selection.
  4. Dock Console next to Project, move Game to sit beside Scene, and save layout as "MyCustomLayout".
Quick visual mnemonics
Scene = sandbox. Game = final camera view.
Hierarchy = parent-child structure; children inherit transforms.
Key Takeaway

Do the short checklist twice: first to observe, second to internalize the keybindings and window roles.

screens.title: Core Windows: Purpose and Relationships
screens.subtitle: Understand what each main Editor window is for and how they work together

narration.text: Let's define the six core windows and how they interact so you can choose the right window for each task. First, the Scene view is an interactive workspace where you place and arrange GameObjects. Think of it as a staging area where you can move lights, models, and cameras freely. The Game view shows what the player will see through the active camera — it's the runtime rendering including lighting and UI. A key relationship to understand is that edits in the Scene view update the Game view when not running; they are two perspectives of the same scene state. The Hierarchy lists every GameObject present in the active scene and reveals parent-child relationships. Parents pass transforms to children, which is how moving a vehicle object moves attached wheels. The Project window holds assets stored in your project's Assets folder — drag items from Project into the Scene or Hierarchy to instantiate them. The Inspector shows properties and components of the selected object; it is the place to tune numerical values and component settings. The Console displays logs, warnings, and errors and helps you trace problems. A common misconception is treating the Game view as an editing canvas; it is for testing only. Example: import a 3D model in Project, drag it into Scene, confirm it appears in Hierarchy, select it and adjust scale in Inspector, then review the final look in Game view. Key takeaway: each window has a clear role and they form a workflow chain: Project -> Scene/Hierarchy -> Inspector -> Game -> Console for feedback. How will you use this chain in your next task?

keyIdea.title: Windows form a workflow chain
keyIdea.text: Project assets move into Scene/Hierarchy, Inspector tunes properties, Game shows runtime result, and Console reports feedback.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Core Windows
Window Roles
Scene View
Interactive 3D workspace for arranging objects and composing levels.
Game View
Player's camera output used to preview rendering and UI at runtime.
Hierarchy
Lists scene GameObjects and parent-child relationships that determine transform inheritance.
Inspector, Project & Console
Inspector
Shows components and properties of selected object; edit values to change behavior or appearance.
Project
Asset browser reflecting the Assets folder. Drag assets into Scene or Hierarchy to instantiate.
Console
Displays Debug.Log information, warnings, and errors. Use it to trace and fix issues as you test.
Key Takeaway

Each window has a single strong purpose; combine them in sequence to build, test, and debug efficiently.

screens.title: Scene View Navigation Controls
screens.subtitle: Orbit, pan, zoom, and frame selection to inspect and position objects

narration.text: Navigation in the Scene view is a core skill. Define each control and practice the exact gestures until they are instinctive. Orbiting lets you turn the camera around a point so you can inspect a model from every angle. On a typical setup you hold the right mouse button and move the mouse to look around; combine this with WASD keys to fly through the scene for broad adjustments. Panning shifts the view sideways or up and down without rotating the camera — use the middle mouse button or Alt plus the left mouse button to pan when finer repositioning is needed. Zooming moves the camera closer or farther with the scroll wheel or by dollying forward using W while looking. Frame selection by pressing F centers and zooms the view on a selected object; this is essential when you lose an object off-screen. A concrete example: select the Main Camera in Hierarchy, press F to frame it, then orbit to check its orientation, and finally press the scroll wheel to zoom to a comfortable distance before tweaking its Transform. A common misconception is confusing Game view navigation with Scene navigation; Game view is for preview only and doesn't provide the same navigation affordances. Practice these controls in brief daily drills until they become reflexive. How will you practice them this session?

keyIdea.title: Make navigation reflexive
keyIdea.text: Use orbit, pan, zoom, and frame selection fluently so you can precisely position and inspect objects without breaking flow.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Scene Navigation
Camera Controls
Orbit
Right mouse + move. Rotates view around current pivot so you can inspect models from all angles.
Pan
Middle mouse or Alt + left drag. Shifts the camera without rotating so alignment stays intact.
Zoom / Dolly
Scroll wheel to zoom; combine with W/S keys for dolly motion when precise depth adjustments are needed.
Frame Selection (F)
Centers the camera on a selected object. Use it when an item is off-screen or too small to locate quickly.
Practice Drill
Step 1
Select the Main Camera in Hierarchy and press F to frame it.
Step 2
Orbit with the right mouse till you see the object from multiple angles, then pan to align it with the horizon.
Step 3
Scroll to zoom in, then press F again if you lose the object. Repeat until the sequence is natural.
Key Takeaway

Short, repeated drills build the reflexes needed to inspect scenes quickly and accurately.

screens.title: Transform Tools: Move, Rotate, Scale
screens.subtitle: Manipulate GameObjects visually and verify values in the Transform component

narration.text: Transforms are the fundamental properties that determine an object's position, rotation, and scale in the scene. Unity exposes three primary tools for editing these: Move, Rotate, and Scale, each with a keyboard shortcut: W, E, and R. Use the Move tool to drag an object along axes; notice the gizmo handles that constrain movement to X, Y, or Z. The Rotate tool provides circular handles for adjusting orientation, and the Scale tool changes size along axes or uniformly. Every visual edit updates the Transform component in the Inspector so you can switch between visual manipulation and precise numeric entry. A concrete example: create a Cube, press W to move it up by dragging the Y handle, then look at the Y position field in the Inspector to see the numeric change; press E and rotate it 45 degrees around Y and confirm the rotation values. A common misconception is expecting transforms to persist when made during Play Mode. Remember that Play Mode changes are temporary and will revert when you stop playing. Also be careful with parent-child relationships: scaling a parent affects all children, which can unintentionally distort nested geometry. The learner takeaway is to use the tools for quick composition and the Inspector for precise tuning — both together make editing reliable and repeatable.

keyIdea.title: Use tools + Inspector together
keyIdea.text: Visual gizmos speed composition; the Transform in the Inspector provides precise numeric control and confirms changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Transform Tools
Tool Definitions
Move (W)
Drag axis handles to adjust position. Use the Inspector for exact coordinates.
Rotate (E)
Rotate around axes with circular gizmos; watch rotation values update in the Inspector.
Scale (R)
Resize uniformly or per-axis; remember parent scaling affects children.
Concrete Example
Create a Cube
1) GameObject > 3D Object > Cube. 2) Press W, drag Y handle up. 3) Verify Y value in Inspector changed. 4) Press E, rotate 45 degrees around Y and confirm.
Common Mistake

Editing transforms in Play Mode seems to work but will be lost when you stop. Make permanent edits outside Play Mode.

screens.title: Hierarchy Window & Parent-Child Relationships
screens.subtitle: Organize scene objects and understand transform inheritance

narration.text: The Hierarchy window lists all GameObjects present in your active scene in a tree structure. This structure reflects parent-child relationships that are essential for organization and behavior. When an object is parented to another, it inherits position, rotation, and scale changes from that parent. For example, if you have a vehicle GameObject with wheels as children, moving the vehicle moves the wheels automatically because the children's transforms are relative to the parent's coordinate space. Use empty GameObjects as parents to group related objects and to create logical control roots for movement or animation. A common beginner error is parenting objects without considering how local transforms will change; children keep local values but their world transforms change as the parent moves or scales. Concrete practice: create an empty GameObject named "VehicleRoot", create a Cube as a child and observe how its Transform values display local coordinates in the Inspector. Then move VehicleRoot and watch the child's world position update visually while its local values remain. Keep your Hierarchy tidy with clear names and grouping folders like Models, Lights, and UI so you can find and select objects quickly. A clean Hierarchy speeds development and reduces accidental edits.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy organizes and propagates transforms
keyIdea.text: Use parent objects to group related parts; children inherit transformations which simplifies complex movement but requires careful naming and structure.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hierarchy & Parenting
Parent-Child Model
The Hierarchy displays GameObjects as a nested tree. Parents provide a coordinate frame for children. Use empty GameObjects as organizational roots and to control groups of objects together.
Example: Vehicle
VehicleRoot (parent) with WheelFL, WheelFR, Body as children. Moving VehicleRoot moves all wheels and body together.
Local vs World
Children show local Transform values in the Inspector; world position changes when the parent moves even if local values stay the same.
Practice
Step
Create an empty GameObject named VehicleRoot and a Cube as child. Move VehicleRoot and observe child's world movement while its local values remain.
Tip
Use clear naming and folder-like grouping to avoid selection mistakes and accidental parenting.
Common Mistake

Scaling a parent can unexpectedly distort children; check child geometry after large parent scale changes.

screens.title: Project Window: Asset Organization and Importing
screens.subtitle: Keep your Assets folder structured and learn quick import workflows

narration.text: The Project window is your asset browser and the single source of truth for files inside the Assets folder. It lists models, textures, audio, scripts, and prefabs. A clear folder structure — for example Scripts, Models, Materials, Audio — prevents confusion as the project grows. Importing assets is simple: drag files from your operating system explorer into the Project window and Unity will import them into Assets. When you drag an asset into the Scene or Hierarchy you instantiate it; this creates a scene object that references the asset. A practical example: import a 3D model into Project, then drag it into the Scene to create a GameObject and inspect its imported material and scale settings. Use the search bar and filters to find assets quickly, and right-click context menus to reveal import settings. Keep naming consistent and avoid deep nested folders that make files hard to locate. A common misconception is thinking Project contains scene instances; it does not — it stores reusable asset files. If you delete an asset from Project that is referenced in scenes, Unity will break those references. Key practice: create a clear folder scheme at project start and use prefabs for reusable objects so you can update prototypes globally rather than editing instances individually.

keyIdea.title: Project holds source assets
keyIdea.text: Organize Assets with consistent folders, import via drag-and-drop, and use prefabs to manage reusable content across scenes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Project Window
Asset Management
Treat the Project window as the repository for all source files. Create clear top-level folders for Scripts, Models, Materials, Audio, and Scenes. Avoid long, deep folder trees that make items hard to locate.
Importing
Drag files from your OS into Project to import. Then drag assets into Scene or Hierarchy to instantiate them.
Prefabs
Use prefabs for reusable objects so you can update the original and propagate changes to instances.
Concrete Example
Import & Place Model
1) Drag a model into Project. 2) Drag model from Project into Scene. 3) Select instance and inspect material and scale settings in Inspector.
Common Pitfall

Deleting assets from Project removes the source file and can break scenes that reference it. Use version control and a clear folder policy.

screens.title: Inspector Window: Components and Properties
screens.subtitle: Read and change components to configure GameObjects without code

narration.text: The Inspector is the place where you read and edit the properties of a selected GameObject or asset. Every GameObject has a Transform component and zero or more other components such as Mesh Renderer, Rigidbody, Collider, or custom scripts. When you select a GameObject, the Inspector shows its full component list and the editable fields for each. Editing values here is the primary way designers and programmers configure behavior without recompiling. A practical example: select a Cube and expand the Mesh Renderer to adjust material settings, or add a Rigidbody component and tune mass and drag to change physics behavior. The Inspector also shows import settings for assets — for instance, selecting a texture reveals options like compression and max size. A common misconception is cluttering the Inspector with too many components; prefer composition over sprawling single objects, and use prefabs to manage complexity. If you add script-exposed variables, they appear in the Inspector when serialized, making tuning easier. Key takeaway: use the Inspector both for rapid experimentation and for precise configuration, but remember to make permanent edits outside Play Mode to avoid losing changes.

keyIdea.title: Inspector is the configuration hub
keyIdea.text: Use it to tune components, view import settings, and expose script variables for rapid iteration — but edit permanently outside Play Mode.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Inspector
Components & Properties
Inspect and edit components attached to GameObjects. Components encapsulate behavior and data; the Transform is always present. Adding or removing components changes the GameObject's capabilities.
Script Variables
Public or serialized fields in scripts show up in the Inspector for tuning without code changes.
Asset Import Settings
Selecting an asset shows import options such as texture compression or model scale which affect how it appears at runtime.
Concrete Example
Add a Rigidbody
Select Cube, click Add Component > Physics > Rigidbody, then adjust mass and drag. Test behaviour in Play Mode to see physics react to forces.
Warning

Avoid relying on Play Mode edits. Use Inspector edits outside Play Mode for changes you want to keep.

screens.title: Scene View vs Game View — Editing vs Preview
screens.subtitle: Know the difference and how Play Mode affects your edits

narration.text: Understanding the difference between Scene and Game views prevents wasted work. The Scene view is an editing canvas where you can freely manipulate objects, lights, and cameras. The Game view renders the scene from the active camera perspective and shows how the player will see the world with runtime effects applied. A crucial point: editing in Play Mode is temporary. When you enter Play Mode, Unity creates a runtime instance of your scene. Any changes made while playing—moving objects, changing values, or adding components—are applied to the temporary play instance and are discarded when you exit Play Mode. This is a common source of frustration: you tweak a value, see a better result while playing, then stop and find the tweak gone. The correct workflow is to note desired changes while playing, then pause or exit Play Mode and make those edits in edit mode so they persist. Concrete example: while testing, you may increase a cube's scale to test spacing; record the value and reapply it after stopping play, or copy the value from the Inspector before exiting. Key takeaway: use Play Mode for experimentation and the Scene view plus Inspector for persistent edits.

keyIdea.title: Play Mode is ephemeral
keyIdea.text: Use Play Mode to test ideas but apply lasting changes outside Play Mode in the Scene view and Inspector.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Scene vs Game
Edit vs Preview
Scene View
Editing canvas for arranging and tuning objects. Edits here persist when not in Play Mode.
Game View
Runtime preview showing camera output and runtime effects; use it to validate player experience.
Practical Rule
Treat Play Mode as a sandbox. Note desirable changes during Play, then stop and apply them in Edit Mode to make them permanent.
Example
Increase a jumpForce in Play Mode to test feel. Record the value and then set it in the Inspector after exiting Play Mode so the change persists.
Common Frustration

Many learners lose edits after testing because they forget to reapply changes made in Play Mode. Use a quick note or copy values before exiting.

screens.title: Customize and Save Editor Layouts
screens.subtitle: Dock, float, and save workspace arrangements for different tasks

narration.text: Customizing the Editor layout tailors Unity to your task and reduces friction. Every window can be docked, floated, or rearranged by dragging its tab. Common layouts include a level design view with Scene and Game side-by-side, or a scripting layout with a large Project window and Console visible. After arranging windows, save your configuration via Window > Layouts > Save Layout and give it a descriptive name like "LevelDesign" or "Scripting". The main benefit is repeatability: switching layouts restores a previously optimized workspace and avoids repetitive manual rearranging. A concrete workflow: move the Console next to the Project window so logs are visible while importing assets, then save the layout as "ImportReview". A practical pitfall is relying on a layout while in Play Mode if you forget Play Mode resets temporary state; layouts persist, but Play Mode changes to objects do not. Another common issue is overflowing windows on smaller displays — test your saved layout on the target screen size. Key takeaway: create a few named layouts fit for common tasks and switch between them to streamline context switching and reduce setup time.

keyIdea.title: Layouts improve focus
keyIdea.text: Save named layouts for recurring tasks so your workspace matches the job and helps you stay productive.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Customize Layouts
Layout Actions
Dock & Float
Drag window tabs to dock them in different positions or float them as separate windows for multi-monitor setups.
Save Layout
Use Window > Layouts > Save Layout to record your arrangement with a descriptive name for reuse.
Use Cases
Level Design
Scene + Game side-by-side with Inspector and Hierarchy visible for rapid placement and testing.
Scripting
Project, Console, and Inspector prominent so you can edit scripts and see errors quickly.
Key Takeaway

Save several named layouts for common tasks to reduce context switching and setup time.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: These three compact concepts encapsulate the chapter. First, the Editor is a workspace with distinct windows each fulfilling specific roles: Scene for building, Game for preview, Hierarchy for structure, Project for assets, Inspector for configuration, and Console for feedback. Second, camera and transform controls are muscle memory skills: orbit, pan, zoom, frame selection, and Move/Rotate/Scale tools let you position and tune objects quickly. Practice them to reduce friction. Third, Play Mode is ephemeral; use it for testing and experimentation but apply persistent changes in Edit Mode. Saving named layouts and organizing assets with a clear folder scheme further helps you maintain a predictable and efficient workflow. Keep these three ideas in mind as you develop: organized assets, practiced navigation, and careful Play Mode habits. Which of these will you focus on practicing first?

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Windows have purposes, navigation is a reflex, and Play Mode changes are temporary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Concepts
Editor Windows
Each window serves a distinct purpose; use them together as a workflow chain.
Navigation & Tools
Practice orbit, pan, zoom, and the W/E/R tools until they are second nature.
Play Mode Caution
Use Play Mode for testing only; apply permanent changes outside Play Mode.
Summary Takeaway

Build a small, repeatable workflow: organize assets, practice navigation and transforms, and save named layouts so development is fast and predictable.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact practical rules for daily use

narration.text: Keep three practical rules in mind as you work: first, always organize assets in the Project window with a predictable folder scheme; it prevents confusion later. Second, use the Hierarchy thoughtfully—group objects under parent roots to control sets of objects together but be mindful how parent transforms affect children. Third, adopt a simple workflow for testing: use Play Mode to experiment, then reapply confirmed changes in Edit Mode so they persist. These rules make collaboration, debugging, and iteration smoother. As a short exercise, pick one rule and apply it immediately: create a Scripts folder in Project, group related GameObjects under a parent in the Hierarchy, or practice copying a value from the Inspector after testing in Play Mode. Small, repeated habits compound into reliable workflows that keep your projects maintainable and your sessions productive. Which rule will you adopt as part of your next editing session?

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Organize assets, structure hierarchy, and treat Play Mode edits as temporary experiments.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What to Remember
Organize Project
Start with top-level folders: Scripts, Models, Materials, Audio. Keep names consistent.
Structure Hierarchy
Group related objects under parent GameObjects for easier movement and control.
Play Mode Rule
Use Play Mode to test ideas, then reapply successful changes in Edit Mode to save them.
Next Step

Pick one rule and practice it in your next session: organize a folder, restructure a Hierarchy, or solidify a Play Mode change into Edit Mode.
